extracted.intended_audience: public company registrants and GHG emissions attestation providers (and their auditors/advisors)
extracted.subtask_description: Regulatory requirements and evaluation criteria for GHG emissions attestation reports, acceptable standards, provider qualifications, oversight, report contents, and related disclosures that registrants and assurance providers must follow under the SEC's final climate disclosure rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledgement letter / exhibit filing requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Registrant must file the letter from the GHG emissions attestation provider as an exhibit (acknowledgement letter), with instruction to Item 1506 directing registrants obtaining limited assurance to Item 601(b)(27) (and to Form 20-F Instructions as to Exhibits paragraph 18 where applicable).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This requirement follows from similar contexts in prior SEC guidance; it provides notice to the assurance provider and imposes less burden than a consent requirement. Instruction to Item 1506 facilitates compliance by pointing limited-assurance providers to Item 601(b)(27) and related Form 20-F exhibit instructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceptable attestation standards (flexibility)
rubrics_metrics.description: The rule does not prescribe a single attestation standard; it recognizes that more than one suitable attestation standard exists and that others may develop in the future (e.g., PCAOB, AICPA, IAASB standards).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commission derived proposed requirements largely from AICPA SSAE No. 18 and notes similarity to PCAOB AT-101 and IAASB ISAE 3410. Commenters both supported flexibility (to avoid prescribing a single standard) and requested either a non-exclusive list of acceptable standards or updates to existing standards. The staff will consult with registrants about whether a particular standard meets final-rule requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards must be publicly available and follow due process
rubrics_metrics.description: Attestation/verification standards should be publicly available and established by groups that have followed due-process procedures (broad distribution for public comment and stakeholder input).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commenters noted ISO and similar organizations follow broad stakeholder processes. The Commission emphasized standards developed with due process; registrants and providers should use standards that meet those requirements or consult SEC staff regarding suitability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characteristics of suitable criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Criteria used to evaluate GHG disclosures should have key characteristics such as relevance, objectivity, measurability, and completeness (and under IAASB ISAE 3000 also reliability, neutrality, and understandability).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Commission cites AICPA SSAE No. 18, AT-C §105.A16 and A42 and IAASB ISAE 3000.A23. While different standards list slightly different characteristics, the underlying concepts and objectives are consistent and should guide what qualifies as suitable criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceptability of GHG Protocol methodologies for Scope 1/2
rubrics_metrics.description: If a registrant chooses to disclose Scope 1 and/or Scope 2 emissions pursuant to Item 1505 and leverages GHG Protocol methodologies, those methodologies would qualify as suitable criteria against which such disclosures should be evaluated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Commission agrees with commenters that the GHG Protocol's provisions would be suitable criteria for Scope 1/2 disclosures; see related discussion and citations in the release.

rubrics_metrics.name: Level and scope of engagement (limited vs. reasonable assurance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Attestation engagement must specify level and scope: limited assurance engagements have different requirements from reasonable assurance engagements; testing of and attestation over internal controls are not required for limited assurance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under prevailing attestation standards for limited assurance engagements, testing and attestation over internal controls are not required (AICPA SSAE No. 22, AT-C §210.A16). For reasonable assurance, standards require considering and obtaining an understanding of internal controls, but they do not require an attestation of the effectiveness of internal controls like Sarbanes-Oxley section 404(b). Commenters requested clarification on the level of assurance for historical periods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimum contents of the attestation report
rubrics_metrics.description: Attestation reports should include core contents such as a clear expression of opinion (where applicable), statement explaining items reviewed, findings, list of metrics verified, and a statement of independence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Commission derived report requirements from AICPA and other attestation standards; commenters noted in practice reports commonly include an explanation of items reviewed, findings, metrics verified, and independence statement. Comparisons were drawn to Article 2 of Regulation S-X which requires a clear expression of opinion for financial statements; disclaimers do not satisfy that requirement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provider expertise, licensing, and record-keeping qualifications
rubrics_metrics.description: GHG emissions attestation providers should meet qualifications related to expertise and independence, and commenters recommended adding licensing, oversight, and record-keeping requirements to provider qualifications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some commenters recommended requiring licensure (e.g., CPA) or oversight and record-keeping similar to existing auditor requirements. Others suggested allowing non-accounting firms if they meet appropriate accreditation and oversight requirements. The Commission cited letters requesting that such information be disclosed and/or that oversight be a required qualification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provider independence and disclosure of provider information
rubrics_metrics.description: Registrants should disclose information about the attestation provider that is relevant for investors to assess provider quality, including independence-related information and whether the provider is subject to oversight/inspection programs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commenters (e.g., PwC) stated such information would be beneficial to investors; some asked that existence of an oversight inspection program be a required qualification rather than merely a disclosure item. Regulation cross-references (17 CFR 229.1506(d) and related paragraphs) specify disclosure items.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oversight inspection programs for providers
rubrics_metrics.description: Attestation providers should be subject to, or disclose participation in, appropriate oversight inspection programs (examples include the AICPA peer review program and PCAOB inspection program).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The AICPA peer review program is an example (peer reviews at least once every three years for AICPA members). PCAOB inspections are limited to audits of issuers and registered brokers/dealers and do not include GHG attestation engagements within their scope; commenters did not offer examples of oversight programs that apply to non-accountant providers. The Commission notes oversight programs increase confidence and may be a relevant qualification or disclosure element.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accreditation to recognized accreditation standards (e.g., ISO/ANSI)
rubrics_metrics.description: Commenters recommended requiring attestation/verification bodies to be accredited to recognized standards (e.g., ISO 14064-3, ISO 14065, ISO 14066, or ISO 17029) or recognized accreditation bodies (e.g., ANSI NAB).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some commenters stated ISO standards form the basis for quality auditing of GHG emissions and environmental information and recommended requiring attestation bodies to perform engagements in accordance with those requirements. ANSI NAB described itself as a U.S. accreditation body operating a program for oversight of GHG validation and verification bodies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure of change in attestation provider and disagreements/dismissals
rubrics_metrics.description: Registrants should disclose changes in attestation provider and significant disagreements or likely circumstances for dismissal or disagreement between the registrant and the provider.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commenters recommended modeling such disclosures on Item 304 of Regulation S-K and disclosing the 'most likely circumstances' for dismissal/disagreement and examples. CFA Institute stated it would not object to a requirement to disclose a change in attestation provider. Relevant rule citations include 17 CFR 229.1506(d) and subparagraphs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provision for staff consultation on standard suitability
rubrics_metrics.description: The Commission's Office of the Chief Accountant staff is available to consult with registrants about whether a particular standard meets the final-rule requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where commenters questioned whether particular standards (e.g., AA1000) met due-process or other criteria, the staff offered consultation to registrants to determine if a standard satisfies the rules' requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Derivation of minimum requirements from prevailing attestation standards
rubrics_metrics.description: The Commission primarily derived the proposed minimum report and engagement requirements from prevailing attestation standards (AICPA SSAE No.18, PCAOB AT-101, IAASB ISAE 3410), and therefore the minimum contents/criteria reflect those standards' norms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commenters argued that if the Commission limited acceptable standards to PCAOB/AICPA/IAASB, other minimum criteria could be removed; conversely, if flexibility is maintained, the Commission provided minimum report contents based on those established standards to promote consistency and investor transparency.
